name: Gareth Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Ridgeway Motors in a commuter town, a busy independent garage with four bays. Steve Barker owns it, and I'm one of three mechanics. I start by checking the AI diagnostic reports on the tablet, then it's services, timing belts, suspension, and I write the customer quotes with an AI assistant because it's twice as fast. I love the buzz of a full board, and I hate that I'm still on lower pay than the main dealer pays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you want from the next few years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My own garage, honestly. My granddad had one in the village before he retired, and I spent every Saturday there as a boy. I rent a flat above a bakery and I've got under a month's money saved, so it's a long way off, but I think about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shame. I was hoping the tools would keep getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI helped in small ways and the rest was hype, but the small ways are still worth having. At work I'd keep using it for quotes and diagnosis. Online I'd share the tricks that save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my own garage is further off. I was counting on AI to let one person run a small garage with low overheads. Without that, I'm just a mechanic on lower pay with three weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI every day for the quotes. I'd ask Steve for a raise on the back of the quoting work I do. I'd start saving properly, a hundred a month, towards a deposit on a unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not worried exactly, just impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would it take to save for your own unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small garage unit with a lift and tools is maybe twenty thousand to start, and at a hundred a month that's never. I'd need a business loan, and banks want savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your granddad help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd give me advice, not money, and that's right. He built his garage himself with a bank loan and long hours. I'd want to do the same.

I'd share **time-saving tricks** online for other mechanics.
think: My **own garage** is further off without better AI.
I'm on **lower pay** with three weeks of rent saved.
do: Use AI **daily** for quotes and diagnosis.
Ask Steve for a **raise** based on quoting work.
Save **a hundred a month** towards a unit deposit.

His **traditional** values show in refusing family money.

Save a hundred a month towards a garage unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, and it suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mechanics who learn the tools will thrive and those who don't will struggle. That's how markets work. I'd tell young mechanics to get stuck in now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this makes my own garage possible. If AI does the booking, quoting, ordering and half the diagnosis, one good mechanic can run a small place alone. The risk is Steve using it to cut a mechanic before I'm ready to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Steve to let me run the AI booking and quoting side of Ridgeway Motors for a bit more pay. I'd start doing weekend jobs on the side to save faster. In the first year I'd draw up a plan for my own unit and take it to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with some nerves. It feels like my chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridgeway would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, who's fifty-five and won't touch the tablet. He's a brilliant mechanic, but Steve's a businessman, and he'd cut the slowest earner. I'd try to show Mick the basics, but I can't make him learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want your own garage but you've got three weeks of savings. Is the plan realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. That's why I'd do the side work first and only go when I've got six months of savings. My granddad always said you don't open a garage on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a race now, and those who move fastest will be fine. But I'd also say families need to look after each other, because nobody's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 AI does all the thinking work in a garage, better than me. That makes my AI edge worthless. My hands are worth something until 2031, when robots come, and a garage owner then might just be someone who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd forget opening a garage with a lift and mechanics. I'd look at becoming the person who sets up and repairs the AI kit and robots for local garages. I'd save hard, cut everything, and maybe move back in with my parents for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like the finish line moved before I even started running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does owning the robots mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots do the work, the money goes to whoever owns the robots. I'd want to own a couple, not be replaced by them. But I'd need capital I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the three years before robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to save and train as a robot technician while still earning as a mechanic. If I time it right, I'm the person garages call when their robots break. That's still a kind of garage of my own.

**Families** need to look after each other, because nobody's ready.
think: By **2028** AI does all the garage thinking, and my AI edge is worthless.
A future garage owner may be **whoever owns** the robots.
do: Train to set up and **repair robots** for local garages.

feel: **Anxious**; the finish line moved before I started.
S2.quote: If the robots do the work, the money goes to whoever owns the robots.
fieldNote: Gareth's **free-market** view becomes a wish to own robots, not fight them.
He'd move back with **parents**, leaning on family.
He reframes his dream as a **robot repair** business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Now that I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this gives enough time for those who want to work hard and learn. I'd say apprenticeships should teach robot repair now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to open a small garage, run it with AI for a few years, and then switch to robot servicing by 2034. I'd be thirty-four. That's young enough to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do weekend jobs for two years and save. In year three I'd open a small unit run with AI for bookings and quotes. Along the way I'd do a robotics maintenance course so I'm ready for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a motivated way. It feels like a plan I can actually follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bank says no to a loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd start as a mobile mechanic with a van first, which is cheaper. I'd build up customers and try the bank again later. You don't give up because the bank says no once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice, yes, and I'd teach them the robot side from day one. That's how my granddad taught me, side by side.

think: Five years lets me **open a garage** and then switch to robots.
At **thirty-four** I'm young enough to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's perfect timing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd tell people to stop waiting for government and start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years means I can open my own garage, run it with AI for years, and then buy a couple of robots when they come in 2039. I'd be forty, with a business, maybe a family. This is the one where I win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for two years, then open a small unit. I'd use AI for everything except the hands-on work. I'd plan to buy robots once they're proven, not first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. The thin savings worry me now, but not the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from your granddad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My granddad did the books himself until midnight; I'd let the AI do the books so I can go home. That's the one thing I'd change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to marry and have kids by thirty-five, and own the garage first. Ten years gives me time to do both in the right order.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My AI edge would be worthless before I'd saved a penny, and robots would come before I could own any. What would help is small business loans for tradespeople and apprenticeships in robot repair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about ownership. People talk about robots taking jobs, but the question is who owns them. A mechanic who owns two robots is a business owner; a mechanic who owns none is out of work.

headlineQuote: A mechanic who owns two robots is a business owner; a mechanic who owns none is out of work.
portrait: Gareth, 27, works at a **busy garage** and uses AI daily for quotes and diagnosis.
He dreams of his **own garage**, like his granddad's, but has three weeks of rent saved.
He's **free-market** and traditional, wanting enterprise over handouts.
He sees Steady Disruption and slower AGI as his **chance**, planning a garage then robots.
In AGI by 2028 he'd move home and train in **robot repair**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which makes his AI edge worthless before he can own robots.
